Third quarter vs. TipRanks consensus:
▪️ Non-GAAP EPS $2.09 vs. $1.95, up 74% from a year ago
▪️ Revenue $13.38B vs. $13.1B, up 45%, and $77M above the top of AMD’s own guide range
▪️ Data Center a record $8.55B, up 97%, vs. $8.2B expected per Bloomberg
▪️ Client $2.95B, up 7%, a hair under the $3.0B FactSet estimate
▪️ Gaming $773M, down 40% but well above the $634M estimate; Embedded $1.11B, up 29%

Data Center added $4.2B, 102% of AMD’s $4.1B revenue increase. Everything else combined shrank 1.5%. Data Center now earns 74% of segment operating income on 64% of revenue, and its operating margin rose 9 points to 33.7%.

Some other quibbles:
▪️ Free cash flow fell 64% to $554M, about half the $1.05B expected and a 4% margin vs. 17% a year ago, as working capital absorbed $3.4B. The biggest piece was a $3.0B inventory build; inventory is up 45% since December to $11.5B.

▪️ GAAP EPS of $1.46 absorbed a $1.1B charge on warrants issued to customers. That liability rises with the share price.

The hyperscaler math: Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent $208.8B on capex last quarter. AMD’s Data Center revenue was 4.1% of that, so each point of share is worth about $2.1B a quarter.

To watch: fourth-quarter cash flow, inventory, and the margin step-down.

Goldman’s Risk Appetite Indicator* which made a lot of headlines the prior week falling to the least since April 2025 rebounded to −0.3 from −0.5, snapping a four-week losing streak, and the momentum index edged up to −0.8 from −0.9.

Under the hood, credit remains the weak spot. Its sub-component bounced to −2.0, but the prior week it fell to about −3, well below its April 2025 low (around −1.8) and the lowest since at least the start of 2025 (where the chart begins). Equities recovered to around flat (−0.1). 

Goldman’s asset allocation team adds that cross-asset sentiment and positioning “are back to more neutral levels,” and its equity tail-risk model “still points to a less negative asymmetry… but with worsening signal from the business cycle and sentiment.”

*"Goldman Sachs Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) aims to track the level of global market risk appetite and risk aversion based on various market variables. A sharp rise in the index can send a warning signal that investors have more risk appetite and are potentially exposed to a correction if consensus views are tested. Similarly, a sharp decline indicates a reduction in risk appetite, and at extreme levels it can indicate that markets may have overshot. RAI signals are most powerful when the level of risk appetite is very low below -1.5, with levels closer to -2.0 giving the clearest signal over longer time horizons, as at such levels the asymmetry of subsequent medium term equity return becomes very positively skewed. RAI momentum is designed to track short term shifts of market risk appetite, and subcomponents of the RAI.”

September JOLTS strong across the board: openings rise the most since May, hires up the most since March, quits the most since May 2023, and layoffs the least since March 2025.

▪️ Openings: up 333,000 to 7.52 million, the highest since May, beating the 7.10 million consensus by more than 400,000 (August revised up 111,000). There were 1.06 openings per unemployed worker, above 1.0 for a sixth straight month.
▪️ Hires: up 131,000 to 5.40 million, the highest since March, with the hires rate at 3.4%. Hires minus separations, an employment proxy, was 83,000, against a 29,000 gain in September payrolls.
▪️ Quits: up 321,000, the most since May 2023, to 3.37 million, the highest since March 2025, and the quits rate rose to 2.1% from 1.9%. Accommodation and food services accounted for 197,000 of it; excluding that though industry quits still rose 124,000 the most since March 2025
▪️ Layoffs: down 127,000 to 1.64 million, the lowest since March 2025, with the rate at 1.0%. The catch: August was revised up 127,000, turning its reported decline into a 66,000 increase.

Revisions also undid two of last month’s stories. The August drop in openings at the smallest firms shrank to 152,000 from 335,000, and August private-sector hires now show a 76,000 gain rather than a decline.

Fits Fed Chair Warsh’s “quite positive” read on employment. It also gives the hawks more firepower although a lot more data before the December 8-9 meeting.

Traders Sell China's Latest Effort to Put a Floor Under Markets

A little under the radar, China’s benchmark CSI 300 equity index fell 8.5% in October, its worst month since January 2016 (−21.0%), narrowly beating the October 2018 (−8.3%) at the height of the trade war. It also fell for a record 12 straight weeks through Friday, per Bloomberg. The index is down 15% this year.

As @C_Barraud notes in his Tuesday Brief this happened despite state-fund buying since July and earlier curbs on share sales. So Beijing returned to the toolbox Monday:

▪️ The PBOC cut the rate on its buyback/stake-increase relending facility to 1% from 1.25% and made it permanent. About 440 billion yuan of those loans have been contracted, with more than 280 billion disbursed.
▪️ It is restarting the swap facility that lets brokers, funds and insurers swap assets for liquidity to buy stocks. 31 firms are approved and have applied for more than 100 billion yuan of quotas. Operations start in the coming days (outstanding balance is 105 billion).
▪️ The CSRC will make buybacks easier, including when shares trade below their IPO price, and is studying looser margin-financing rules.
▪️ Per the FT, regulators gave banks “window guidance” to pause IPOs and suspended large share sales by existing holders until markets recover.
▪️ Bloomberg says turnover in national-team-favored ETFs jumped to 120 billion yuan, the highest since late January, which suggests the state stepped in directly.

The market was less than impressed. The tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8% on Tuesday, wiping out Monday’s anticipation rally. The CSI 300 was down as much as 1.2% before closing down 0.2%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.6%.

Why it isn’t working: these are the September 2024 tools without the September 2024 punch. Back then the facilities came with rate cuts, and the CSI 300 jumped about 21% in a single month. This time there is no rate cut, and as one Shanghai CIO told Bloomberg, the tools have been around for two years and add no new support. Capital Economics says a lasting turnaround needs earnings growth, which near term means monetary or fiscal support.

History on IPO freezes isn’t encouraging either. Beijing halted listings in early July 2015, and the CSI 300 still fell 14.7% that month and another 11.8% in August before it found a floor.

What to watch: whether the PBOC adds a policy-rate or reserve-requirement cut (the missing piece compared with 2024), how fast the swap quotas are drawn down, and whether national-team ETF volume stays elevated.

It sort of passed under the radar, but last week after 13 years the Bank of Japan says underlying inflation has finally reached its 2% target, the goal it set in January 2013 and once expected to hit in about two years. Still, the BOJ held at 1.25% on an 8-1 vote, with only hawk Takata dissenting for a hike, and Governor Ueda kept December firmly in play.

The new Outlook Report leans hawkish:
▪️ Core CPI forecast (ex-fresh food) for fiscal 2027 raised to 2.6% from 2.4%; fiscal 2026 unchanged at 2.5%
▪️ Ex-fresh food and energy peaks at 2.7% in fiscal 2027
▪️ Risks to prices judged skewed to the upside
▪️ Growth stuck around 0.7% a year
▪️ ETF sales nearly triple to about ¥860 billion a year, cutting the unwind to 43 years from 110+

The hold was even as the BOJ is still deeply accommodative. At 1.25%, the policy rate is about -1.35% in real terms against Tokyo’s 2.6% core reading.

 Bloomberg Economics sees hikes in December, March and July to 2%, the top of ING’s 1.75% to 2.00% neutral range. Even then, the real rate would be about -0.6% against the board’s own fiscal 2027 forecast.

For the yen, the Fed-BOJ gap is roughly half its mid-2024 level, yet the yen is only about 3% off its weakest levels. If both the Fed and the BOJ hike in December, the gap doesn’t narrow, which fits ING’s call for a 155 to 160 range.
